endorsements.quote: When surveillance and validation indicate persistent, nonmitigable risk, governance should support staged controls: conditional suspension (use restricted to defined contexts), rollback to a prior validated version, and decommissioning or recall when risks cannot be acceptably reduced.
By design, surveillance does not “reprove” effectiveness; it detects deviations and triggers targeted validation when thresholds are crossed.

Co-Lifecycle Governance therefore emphasizes traceability: a chain of custody for model versions, validation evidence, deployment context, and corrective actions, which supports both clinical trust and legal enforceability [ 25-28 ].

Surveillance is primarily passive and signal-oriented: it continuously tracks aggregate and subgroup performance proxies (eg, drift metrics, calibration signals, alert rates, and incident reports) to identify anomalies that warrant investigation [ 1 , 7 , 8 ].

Continuous validation must reassess these explainability properties after substantial model or interface changes, and performance surveillance should treat systematic clinician confusion, abnormal override patterns, or unexplained subgroup performance shifts as safety signals.

unlisted_practices: Condition initial deployment and any material recalibration or postmarket update on evidence that the system provides interpretable outputs, uncertainty signals, and traceable decision pathways sufficient for clinicians to understand its basis, confidence, and limits.
Do not deploy AI systems that cannot meet explainability conditions, or restrict them to narrower use contexts.
Treat version transparency, minimum performance floors, and update dissemination policies as ethical and operational requirements.
Classify AI changes by risk and regulatory impact, prespecify validation evidence proportional to each change category, and maintain audit-ready documentation preserving traceability across updates.
Structure continuous validation across short-horizon monitoring, intermediate proxy-outcome validation, and longer-horizon confirmation when ground truth is delayed.
Allocate the financial, technical, and organizational burdens of life cycle oversight proportionately across developers, institutions, and regulators, for example through cost-sharing mechanisms.
Preplan and institutionally integrate exit strategies such as rollback and decommissioning, accounting for EHR technical dependencies and workflow disruption.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint proposing a conceptual framework (Co-Lifecycle Governance) and recommendations for adaptive regulatory oversight and governance of learning AI in healthcare.
